title: Tingling and cramps after thyroid surgery — recognise, investigate and act safely

blocks.text: Tingling and cramps after thyroid surgery — recognise, investigate and act safely

AMaC MRCP PACES23 | Round 5 | R5-238 | Station 2: acute consultation | 20 minutes | Communication, clinical judgement and patient welfare (C, E, F, G) | AMaC educational scoring, not official PACES marks
A 42-year-old develops tingling around the mouth, hand cramps and muscle spasms on the day after total thyroidectomy. Take a focused history, determine urgency and explain your plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: Hook: Symptomatic postoperative hypocalcaemia, commonly due to transient parathyroid dysfunction. Chvostek and Trousseau signs are supportive but not sufficiently sensitive or specific to rely upon. Trap: Correct magnesium where low and monitor for recurrent hypocalcaemia; do not administer IV calcium unmonitored.

rows: “First, I want to check how unwell you are.”
Assess stability and the specific emergency signs.
“I’ll ask questions that help us distinguish the causes.”
Ask onset, spasms, stridor, seizures, previous calcium problems and medication. Assess airway, neuromuscular irritability and vital signs; obtain ECG for QT interval.
“I will arrange tests and support appropriate to the risk.”

Urgently check adjusted or ionised calcium, magnesium, phosphate, renal function and PTH where appropriate; give IV calcium gluconate for severe or symptomatic hypocalcaemia under monitoring and local protocol, then arrange oral calcium/active vitamin D plan with endocrinology.
“I will explain when we must act urgently.”
Stridor/laryngospasm, tetany, seizure, arrhythmia or prolonged QT is an emergency: secure airway if threatened and give monitored IV calcium without delay.

blocks.text: Patient is concerned about the symptoms and asks: ““Is this because my thyroid gland was removed?”” The role-player provides symptoms from the brief and relevant positive/negative history only when asked; avoid volunteering the diagnosis. Respond to clear empathetic explanations.
Q1. What is the likely mechanism? — Reduced parathyroid function after surgery leading to low calcium.
Q2. What is dangerous? — Laryngospasm, seizures, tetany and prolonged QT/arrhythmias.
Q3. What must be checked? — Corrected/ionised calcium, magnesium, phosphate, renal function, PTH and ECG.
Q4. When is intravenous treatment appropriate? — Severe or symptomatic hypocalcaemia; monitored calcium gluconate is an emergency treatment.
Q5. What needs ongoing care? — Repeat calcium monitoring, correction of magnesium and appropriate endocrine/surgical follow-up.

THINK: Symptomatic postoperative hypocalcaemia, commonly due to transient parathyroid dysfunction. Chvostek and Trousseau signs are supportive but not sufficiently sensitive or specific to rely upon. SAY: avoid certainty without confirmation. DO: Urgently check adjusted or ionised calcium, magnesium, phosphate, renal function and PTH where appropriate; give IV calcium gluconate for severe or symptomatic hypocalcaemia under monitoring and local protocol, then arrange oral calcium/active vitamin D plan with endocrinology. NUMBERS: 20-minute encounter. TRAP: Correct magnesium where low and monitor for recurrent hypocalcaemia; do not administer IV calcium unmonitored. FINISH: Stridor/laryngospasm, tetany, seizure, arrhythmia or prolonged QT is an emergency: secure airway if threatened and give monitored IV calcium without delay.
